subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Whose hand span measures the table best?

tasks_in_class.description: Discuss and explain what various activities are shown in the party picture.
Discuss how Shelly finds the height of the door.
Will Leena and Adi get the same measurement of the table using their hand spans? Discuss.
Identify all ways children use to measure length in the picture; which way is better and why?

time_bands.activity: Open the party scene picture together. Children take turns naming what the children in the picture are doing — especially any measuring or comparing activity. Use Let us Do Q1, p.128 ("Discuss and explain what various activities are shown....") to anchor the conversation.

Focus on Shelly measuring the door with her hand span. Let us Do Q2, p.128 ("Discuss how Shelly finds the height of the door.") — children mime the action, then share their count aloud. Follow immediately with Let us Do Q3, p.128 ("Will Leena and Adi get the same measurement....") — pairs predict, then one pair from each table demonstrates with an actual desk.

Children choose two or three measuring tools shown in the picture (hand span, footsteps, paper strip) and use them to measure the nearest desk or bench. Record results on the board as a class tally, revealing the variation in counts.

Whole-class discussion anchored in Let us Do Q7, p.128 ("Identify all ways children use to measure length...."). Children vote on which method is 'better' and justify their reasoning in one sentence each.

periods.teacher_notes: The expected discovery is that two children using their own hand spans will get different counts for the same object — the variation in the class tally is the evidence. A common error is that children assume anyone using hand spans will get the same number; press them with 'Would Leena's count and Adi's count match? How do you know?' to surface the inconsistency.
materials: Nearest classroom desks or benches for live demonstration

periods.activity_title: Finding the shortest and longest paper strings

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the child with the longest ponytail.
Tick paper strings in the classroom that are as long as the height of the window.
Colour the shortest paper string red and the longest green; discuss how you identified each.
How many more paper strings are needed to decorate the border of the green board?
How many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border of the board?

time_bands.activity: Quick visual comparison warm-up using Let us Do Q4, p.128 ("Circle the child with the longest ponytail."). Children discuss how they can tell which ponytail is longest without measuring — visual alignment, tracing, or direct comparison.

Children stand at the window and use their own paper strips or outstretched arms to judge which prepared strings displayed in the room are as long as the window height. Let us Do Q5, p.128 ("Tick paper strings in the classroom that are as long as the height of the window.") — record ticks on a shared list on the board.

Coloured-string task: Let us Do Q1, p.129 ("Colour the shortest paper string red and the longest green...."). Pairs compare all displayed strings, order them, then colour the endpoints in their books. Brief pair-share: how did they decide which was longest?

Border problems: Let us Do Q2, p.129 ("How many more paper strings are needed....") followed by Let us Do Q3, p.129 ("How many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border...."). Children work individually, then check with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who build on the discovery that informal units give variable results will understand why placing strings side by side or using a common reference string is more reliable than memory comparison. A frequent error in the border problems is counting only some sides of the board; prompt children to trace a finger all the way around before counting.
materials: Prepared paper strings of varying lengths displayed in the room

periods.activity_title: Cut, paste, draw — reproducing and comparing lengths

tasks_in_class.description: Cut and paste a wool or cotton thread as long as the line given below.
Draw a string longer than the string given below.
Draw a string shorter than the decoration string Shelly and Adi are holding.
Draw the other half of the moustache to match the given half.
Look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out.

time_bands.activity: Each child receives a short length of wool or cotton thread. They cut it to match the printed line in Let us Do Q1, p.130 ("Cut and paste a wool or cotton thread as long as the line given below.") and paste it in their book. The act of physical matching is the anchor experience for this unit.

Drawing tasks: Let us Do Q2, p.130 ("Draw a string longer than the string given below.") and Let us Do Q3, p.130 ("Draw a string shorter than the decoration string...."). Children draw, then lay their thread beside the drawn line to verify. Partner checks each other's drawings.

Symmetry drawing: Let us Do Q4, p.130 ("Draw the other half of the moustache to match the given half."). Children use the thread from Q1 as a straightedge guide if needed. Share a few completed examples under the document camera or by holding them up.
Let us Do Q5, p.130 ("Look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out."). Children explain their reasoning to a partner before sharing whole-class.

periods.teacher_notes: The cut-and-paste task anchors the idea that a thread can carry a length from one object to another — the same principle used in indirect comparison later in the chapter. A common error in the drawing tasks is that children draw lines that are visually 'different' without checking against the reference; encourage them to hold their thread beside the reference line before drawing.
materials: Wool or cotton thread (one arm's length per child)

section_titles: Indirect measurement with a common unit
periods.activity_title: Can the table go through the door? Thread as a go-between

tasks_in_class.description: Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it.

time_bands.activity: Read and discuss the textbook story of Shelly and Adi needing to check if a table fits through the door. Children predict: can you tell without moving the table to the door? Elicit the idea of cutting a thread the width of the table and carrying it to the door.

Demonstrate the thread method with a real object in the classroom — cut a thread to match one dimension of a box or bag, then carry that thread to a gap and check whether it fits. Children observe and explain what they see.

Let us Play, p.132 ("Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it."). Groups of three or four set up a simple bridge with two stacks of books and a gap between them. Each child first guesses whether an object (pencil box, water bottle, book) will pass through, then uses the thread method to verify.

Groups share one object that surprised them — something they thought would fit but did not, or vice versa. Children articulate why the thread method gave a reliable answer when visual guessing did not.

periods.teacher_notes: The core idea is that a thread can carry a measurement across space without moving the original objects — this is indirect comparison. A common error is that children hold the thread loosely when measuring the gap, introducing slack; remind them to pull the thread taut at both ends before judging.
materials: Classroom objects of varying widths (pencil box, water bottle, book, lunch box)
Two equal stacks of books to form the bridge gap

periods.activity_title: Testing body-proportion claims with real data

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q1, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is your head 3 handspans round? True or False.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q2, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is the length of your forearm equal to the length of your feet? True or False.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q3, p.133
tasks_in_class.description: Measure and tick: Is your height equal to the length of your arms wide open? True or False.

time_bands.activity: Read the three body-proportion claims from p.133 aloud. Children vote: true or false for each? Record the class prediction on the board as a tally before any measuring begins.

Pairs measure each other for Are these true for all? Q1, p.133 ("Is your head 3 handspans round?") and Are these true for all? Q2, p.133 ("Is the length of your forearm equal to the length of your feet?"). Each child records True or False in their book based on their own body.

Are these true for all? Q3, p.133 ("Is your height equal to the length of your arms wide open?"). One child stands against the wall while a partner marks arm span and height with a thread. Compare and record. Collect all three results on the board as a class frequency table.

Discuss: Did the claim hold for everyone? Why might results differ across children? Lead children to articulate that body proportions vary from person to person — the same limitation as hand-span measurement.

periods.teacher_notes: The purpose is not to prove claims true or false but to experience the variability of body-based measurement across different people — reinforcing why a standard unit is needed. A common error is that children wrap the thread around their head loosely; ask them to keep the thread snug but not tight for a fair measure.
materials: String or wool thread for measuring

section_titles: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
periods.activity_title: Making a metre rope and placing everyone on the scale

tasks_in_class.description: Measure your height using the one-metre mark on the wall; record friends' names as more or less than one metre.
Circle the tallest among the children shown and discuss how you decided.
Write names of objects around you whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the saree-measuring dialogue from the textbook. Children name the informal tools used (pencil, paper strip, arm) and explain why each was unsatisfactory. Introduce the metre rod; children cut a rope to exactly one metre using it.

Mark a one-metre height on the classroom wall. Each child stands against the wall; a partner notes whether their head is above or below the mark. Record all names in two columns — more than one metre / less than one metre — on the board. Measure your height activity, p.135 ("Measure your height using the one-metre mark on the wall; record friends' names....").

Circle the tallest activity, p.135 ("Circle the tallest among the children shown and discuss how you decided."). Children complete the task in their books, then share their reasoning — focusing on what evidence they used.

Objects table activity, p.136 ("Write names of objects around you whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre."). Children walk around the room, mentally comparing each object to their metre rope, and fill the three columns in their books.

periods.teacher_notes: The metre rope the children cut in the first band is the anchor object for the whole unit — every comparison flows from it. A common error is that children mark height when their heels are not flat on the floor; ask them to stand straight with heels touching the wall before the partner marks.
materials: Rope or thick string (one length per pair, cut to one metre)
Chalk or sticky tape to mark the wall at one metre

section_titles: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Folding the metre rope: half and quarter metre emerge

tasks_in_class.description: Find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table.

time_bands.activity: Each child takes a one-metre rope and folds it in half. Teacher asks: what length is each piece? Children agree on half a metre. Fold one half in half again: what length now? Establish quarter metre. Children label three rope lengths: 1 m, ½ m, ¼ m.

Demonstrate measuring a classroom object (e.g. a window ledge) with the metre rope, then choose the half-metre rope when the full metre overshoots. Discuss: which rope to pick first? Introduce the strategy of starting with the full metre and moving to a shorter rope as needed.

Let us Do Q1, p.137 ("Find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table."). Groups of three measure four or five classroom objects, agree on which rope fits best for each, and fill the table together.
Quick share: groups name one object that needed the quarter-metre rope and explain why.

periods.teacher_notes: The folding sequence makes the sub-units concrete before the table activity demands children choose among them. A common error is that children record an object as 'one metre' when it is slightly less; encourage them to describe it as 'less than one metre' rather than rounding up.
materials: One-metre ropes from the previous cutting activity (or freshly cut in this unit)
Pencils for recording in the table

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Jumping, throwing, and measuring real distances

tasks_in_class.description: Draw a start line and a one-metre line; jump and record which children jump more than a quarter, half, and a full metre.
Throw a ball or disc as far as you can; measure how far the throw was.

time_bands.activity: Mark a start line and a one-metre line on the floor using chalk or tape. Discuss: what does it mean to jump 'more than a quarter metre'? Children point to where on the floor each category ends.

Let us Do Q2, p.137 ("Draw a start line and a one-metre line; jump and record which children jump more than a quarter, half, and a full metre."). Children jump one at a time in small groups; a partner marks the landing point and they use their quarter-metre and half-metre ropes to classify the jump. Results are recorded in the book.

Let us Do Q3, p.137 ("Throw a ball or disc as far as you can; measure how far the throw was."). Children take turns throwing a soft ball or flat disc. Partners measure the distance with the metre rope, using as many lengths as needed, and record the result as 'about X metres' or 'between X and X+1 metres'.
Children compare jump and throw distances across the group: Who jumped the furthest? Whose throw was more than one metre? Brief discussion of results.

periods.teacher_notes: Physical measurement outdoors or in a hall works best here; if space is limited, the corridor outside the classroom is adequate. A common error in measuring throwing distance is placing the rope end at the throwing line rather than at the landing point of the object — clarify before measuring begins.
materials: Chalk or masking tape for marking lines

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Measuring the teacher's height and estimating a metre

tasks_in_class.description: Measure the height of your teacher or parent using a metre-long rope or strip.
Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest.
Cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts did you make?

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.138 ("Measure the height of your teacher or parent using a metre-long rope or strip."). The teacher stands against the wall while two children hold and mark the metre rope up the teacher's height. Class counts how many full metres and estimates the remaining portion.

Let us Do Q2, p.138 ("Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest."). Each child receives a long piece of wool and, without measuring, cuts what they think is one metre. All cut lengths are laid beside the metre rope and compared; the closest estimate is celebrated.

Let us Do Q3, p.138 ("Cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts did you make?"). Children fold a one-metre rope into four equal parts, mark the folds, then cut. They count the cuts, discuss why 4 pieces requires only 3 cuts, and connect this to their earlier folding of the metre rope.
Quick reasoning round: children state the answer to the cuts question in one sentence and justify — 'three cuts because the first cut makes two pieces...' — ensuring the reasoning is explicit.

periods.teacher_notes: The estimation activity in Q2 builds the mental image of 'one metre' that is essential for practical measurement; children who have repeatedly handled the metre rope will estimate more accurately than those who have not. The cuts question is commonly answered as 'four cuts' — draw the rope as a horizontal line with marks to show why only three cuts are needed.
materials: One-metre ropes (one per child or pair)
Long wool or thread for the estimation activity

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Footsteps in a metre and measuring the classroom wall

tasks_in_class.description: How many footsteps fit into a metre rope?
Use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is.

time_bands.activity: Recall the opening of the chapter: children measured the classroom by footsteps and got different counts. Ask: if we lay our metre rope on the floor, how many of your footsteps fit along it? Predict before measuring.

Let us Do Q4, p.138 ("How many footsteps fit into a metre rope?"). Each child lays the metre rope on the floor and walks heel-to-toe along it, counting footsteps. Results are recorded and compared in a class tally on the board, illustrating again that counts differ because feet differ.

Let us Do Q5, p.138 ("Use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is."). Groups of four take turns holding the rope end-to-end along a wall, marking each metre with chalk, and counting. One group measures the front wall, another the side wall. Results are shared with the full class.

Compare the metre-rope result with a quick footstep count of the same wall. Children articulate why the metre-rope measurement is more reliable and consistent across groups — bringing the chapter's core idea to the surface.

periods.teacher_notes: The comparison of footstep count versus metre-rope count for the same wall is the natural payoff of the whole chapter's journey from informal to standard units. A common error when measuring the wall is forgetting to mark where each metre ends before moving the rope; supply chalk or sticky dots for groups to mark as they go.
materials: Chalk or sticky dots for wall marking

section_titles: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
periods.activity_title: Consolidating measurement: varied practice across all sub-units

time_bands.activity: Mixed-ability groups of three revisit the object classification table from Let us Do Q1, p.137, but this time choose three new objects not measured before. Groups decide which rope (metre, half metre, quarter metre) to use first and record their results.

Groups design a short 'measurement challenge' for another group: name three objects in the room and predict which rope will be needed. Groups swap challenges and verify each other's predictions using the ropes.

Individual practice: children solve two short problems from the textbook tasks on pp.137–138 that their group has not yet worked through, choosing from the additional tasks noted in teacher guidance. Teacher circulates and gives targeted feedback.
Class gathers for a final 'what did we learn?' round: children complete the sentence 'A metre rope is better than a hand span because…' orally. A few responses are shared and briefly affirmed.

periods.teacher_notes: This consolidation unit draws on the full arc from informal tools to the metre and its sub-units, giving children a chance to revisit any step they found uncertain. Additional practice for the individual band: Let us Do Q2–Q5, pp.137–138 — direct children to tasks they have not yet completed individually.
materials: One-metre, half-metre, and quarter-metre ropes (one set per group)

items.prompt: Your teacher hangs five paper strings of different lengths on the board. How would you find out which string is as long as the height of the classroom window? Describe what you would do.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Take one string, hold it against the window from the bottom to the top, and see whether it reaches exactly to the top. The string whose ends match the bottom and top of the window is the one that matches the window's height.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Hold each string directly against the window and compare its endpoints to the window's bottom and top edges.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child carry a string to the window and physically hold it up; stretch: ask them to find a second object in the room whose height also matches that string.

exercise.description: Tick paper strings in the classroom that are as long as the height of the window.

items.prompt:
Below is a line. Cut a piece of thread that is exactly as long as this line. Paste it in your book next to the line.
[Draw a horizontal line approximately 8 cm long in the printed paper]

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The pasted thread should sit directly beside the printed line with both ends matching — neither overlapping nor falling short.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Lay the thread along the line so both ends align, then cut and paste.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold the thread at the exact endpoint before cutting; stretch: ask them to cut a second piece that is exactly twice as long.

exercise.description: Cut and paste a wool or cotton thread as long as the line given below.

items.prompt: Look at the picture of a moustache in your textbook (p.130). One half is already drawn. Draw the other half so that both sides look the same.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The drawn half should mirror the given half in shape and size so that the whole moustache looks symmetrical — equal on both sides of the centre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the centre point, then copy each curve of the given half on the opposite side at the same distance from the centre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold the paper along the centre to trace the given half; stretch: ask them to colour both halves the same and check they match by folding.

exercise.description: Draw the other half of the moustache to match the given half.

items.section_title: Indirect measurement with a common unit
items.prompt: Riya wants to know if her pencil box will fit through the gap between two stacks of books without moving the pencil box to the gap. Which is the best way to find out?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask a friend who has a bigger pencil box to try it.

options.label: B
options.text: Cut a thread the same width as the pencil box, then hold that thread across the gap.

options.label: C
options.text: Look at the pencil box and the gap from far away and guess.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure the pencil box with hand spans and measure the gap with footsteps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cut a thread the same width as the pencil box, then hold that thread across the gap — option B.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use a thread to carry the measurement of one object to the location of the other without moving either object.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child relies on visual guessing and has not yet understood that indirect comparison needs a go-between measurement.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has not connected the principle: a different object's size is irrelevant to whether the original pencil box fits.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child uses informal units but two different ones, which cannot be compared reliably — a residual misunderstanding from the hand-span/footstep exploration.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: demonstrate with a real thread and a gap in the classroom; stretch: ask the child to name a second object in the room they could check with the same thread.

exercise.description: Make a bridge using boxes or bags; guess and check which classroom objects can go through it.

items.prompt: Meena wrapped a thread around her head. It took 3 of her hand spans to go all the way round. Ravi did the same thing and it took 4 of his hand spans. What does this tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: Both their heads are exactly the same size.

options.label: B
options.text: Hand spans are a good unit because everyone gets the same count.

options.label: C
options.text: Meena's head is bigger than Ravi's head.

options.label: D
options.text: Ravi's hand is smaller than Meena's hand.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ravi's hand is smaller than Meena's hand — option B. When a smaller unit is used more copies are needed to cover the same length.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A larger count with the same object being measured means the unit used is smaller.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confused the count with the size of the head rather than the size of the unit — a classic informal-unit misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child ignored the different counts entirely and assumed the claim always holds, showing they did not reason from the data.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child drew the opposite conclusion from the activity — different counts are the evidence that hand spans are not a consistent unit.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child re-enact measuring the same book with two different-sized hands to see different counts; stretch: ask what would happen if Ravi had even smaller hands — would the count go up or down?

exercise.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q1, p.133
exercise.description: Measure and tick: Is your head 3 handspans round? True or False.

items.prompt: Ananya says: 'My height and my arm span (arms wide open) are the same length.' How would you check whether this is true for yourself? Describe what you would do step by step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Stand against a wall and have a friend mark your height. Then stand straight and stretch your arms wide; have the same friend mark the total arm span on a thread. Compare the two lengths — if they are the same the claim is true for you.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use a thread to capture each measurement, then compare the two threads directly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use a thread to mark height and another for arm span, then lay both side by side; stretch: ask them to predict whether a taller child will have a longer arm span and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Are these true for all? Q3, p.133
exercise.description: Measure and tick: Is your height equal to the length of your arms wide open? True or False.

items.section_title: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
items.prompt: Look at four children standing next to a one-metre mark on the wall. Priya's head is above the mark, Dev's head is at the mark, Sam's head is below the mark, and Leela's head is just a little below the mark. Which children are more than one metre tall?

options.label: A
options.text: All four children.

options.label: B
options.text: Only Priya.

options.label: C
options.text: Priya and Dev.

options.label: D
options.text: Priya, Dev, and Leela.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Only Priya — option A. Her head is above the one-metre mark, meaning her height exceeds one metre. Dev is exactly one metre; Sam and Leela are less.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each child's head position to the one-metre mark: above means more than one metre, at means exactly one metre, below means less.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child included Dev, not distinguishing 'exactly one metre' from 'more than one metre'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child included Leela, confusing 'just below' with 'above' — a reading-the-mark error.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child did not use the one-metre mark as a boundary at all, perhaps assuming all children in the picture are tall.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child point to the mark on a real wall and compare their own height; stretch: ask which two children are closest in height and how you know.

exercise.description: Measure your height using the one-metre mark on the wall; record friends' names as more or less than one metre.

items.section_title: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
items.prompt: Look around your classroom. Write the name of one object whose length is about one metre, one object whose length is more than one metre, and one object whose length is less than one metre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Answers will vary by classroom; examples — about one metre: a classroom door's width or a standard table's length; more than one metre: the classroom wall, a long bench; less than one metre: a book, a pencil box, a child's arm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each object visually or physically to a one-metre rope to place it in the correct category.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: allow the child to carry a one-metre rope to each object before deciding; stretch: ask them to find one object in each category that would surprise a classmate.

exercise.description: Write names of objects around you whose length is one metre, more than one metre, and less than one metre.

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: Kavya measures the width of a classroom door using her ropes. The full metre rope is too long and the quarter-metre rope is too short. Which rope should she use next?

options.label: A
options.text: Full metre rope again.

options.label: B
options.text: Half-metre rope.

options.label: C
options.text: Quarter-metre rope twice.

options.label: D
options.text: She should use her hand span instead.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Half-metre rope — option B. The width is between a full metre and a quarter metre, so the half-metre rope is the appropriate next choice.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose the rope between the one that was too long and the one that was too short.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child repeats the rope that already did not fit, showing they did not reason from the result.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Using the quarter-metre rope twice gives half a metre — this is mathematically equivalent to B but shows the child does not yet recognise the half-metre rope as a direct tool.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child abandons the standard unit, reverting to an informal tool — the chapter's core misconception to overcome.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: lay all three ropes on the desk and ask the child to point to the one between the too-long and too-short; stretch: ask what they would do if the half metre also did not fit exactly.

exercise.description: Find lengths of different objects using one metre, half metre, and quarter metre ropes; fill the table.

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: Arjun and Priya each use a one-metre rope to measure the length of the same classroom wall. Arjun says the wall is 5 metres long. Priya says the wall is 5 metres long too. Why do they get the same answer this time, when hand spans gave different answers earlier?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: They get the same answer because the metre rope is always the same length — it was made from a standard metre rod. Hand spans differ from person to person, so they give different counts for the same object. A standard unit gives every measurer the same result.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A standard unit such as the metre rope is the same length for everyone, so two people measuring the same object get the same count.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child hold two metre ropes side by side to see they are equal; stretch: ask what would happen if one child's rope had been cut a little short by mistake.

exercise.description: Use a metre rope to find how long a side of the class wall is.

items.prompt: Raj measures the width of the classroom door using his hand span and gets 8. His friend Mia measures the same door and gets 10. The door did not change. Why are the numbers different?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Raj's hand span is wider than Mia's, so fewer hand spans fit across the door for Raj and more fit for Mia. The door is the same width, but because the units (hand spans) are different sizes, the counts are different.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A smaller unit gives a larger count for the same length; different hand spans are different-sized units.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child place a large hand and a small hand side by side to see the size difference, then count how many of each fit along a book; stretch: ask which of the two counts — 8 or 10 — belongs to the person with the larger hand and explain why.

exercise.description: Will Leena and Adi get the same measurement of the table using their hand spans? Discuss.

items.prompt: A classroom has a decorated board with paper strings on it. Shirin says the paper string at the top is the longest. Hari says the string at the bottom is the longest. They are looking at the same board. How should they settle this disagreement?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the teacher which one is longer.

options.label: B
options.text: Count how many colours each string has.

options.label: C
options.text: Take both strings off the board and place them side by side to compare.

options.label: D
options.text: The one that looks longer from across the room is longer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Take both strings off the board and place them side by side — option B. Direct comparison of the two objects settles the question without relying on memory or appearance from a distance.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place objects side by side, aligning one end, to compare lengths directly.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child defers to authority rather than using a measurement strategy — avoids the reasoning step.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child relies on visual appearance from a distance, which can be misleading depending on angle and position.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has confused a visual attribute (colour count) with the length attribute being compared.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child remove and compare two real strings of different lengths; stretch: ask what they would do if the strings could not be removed from the board.

exercise.description: Identify all ways children use to measure length in the picture; which way is better and why?

items.prompt: Five paper strings are hung on a board. The table shows how many unit-strings each one measures.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Paper String | Length in unit-strings |
| Red | 3 |
| Blue | 5 |
| Yellow | 2 |
| Green | 5 |
| Purple | 4 |

options.label: A
options.text: Blue is shorter than Purple.

options.label: B
options.text: Green is shorter than Purple.

options.label: C
options.text: Red is the longest.

options.label: D
options.text: Yellow is the shortest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yellow is the shortest — option B. Yellow measures 2 unit-strings, which is the smallest count in the table.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the counts in the table; the smallest count is the shortest string.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child chose Red (3 unit-strings) as longest, perhaps focusing on the first row rather than comparing all values.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child reversed the comparison: Green (5) is equal to Blue (5) and longer than Purple (4), not shorter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child reversed the comparison: Blue (5) is longer than Purple (4), not shorter.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child underline the numbers and circle the smallest; stretch: ask which two strings are the same length and how they know.

exercise.description: Colour the shortest paper string red and the longest green; discuss how you identified each.

items.prompt: A rectangular green board has a top edge that measures 4 unit-strings and a side edge that measures 3 unit-strings. Some unit-strings are already placed along the border. How many more unit-strings are needed to go all the way around the border?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The full border needs 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 unit-strings. Check by tracing all four sides: top 4, right 3, bottom 4, left 3 — total 14.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the unit-string counts for all four sides of the rectangle: top + right + bottom + left.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child draw the rectangle and write the count on each side before adding; stretch: ask how many unit-strings would be needed if the board were one unit-string wider on each side.

exercise.description: How many more paper strings are needed to decorate the border of the green board?

items.prompt: Three string lights are hanging at a party. Light X is short and wiggly. Light Y is long and straight. Light Z is medium length and slightly curved. Adi wants the longest string light. Which should he choose and what is the best way to be sure?

options.label: A
options.text: Choose X because wiggly strings look longer.

options.label: B
options.text: Choose Y and check by straightening all three lights and placing them side by side.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose Z because it is in the middle.

options.label: D
options.text: It is impossible to compare string lights of different shapes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Choose Y and verify by straightening all three and placing them side by side — option B. Straightening removes the distortion caused by curves or wiggles before comparing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Straighten curved or wiggly strings before placing them side by side for a fair comparison.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child was misled by the visual appearance of the wiggly shape, not recognising that curves do not add true length.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child chose the middle option without reasoning — a guess rather than a strategy.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child assumed shape prevents comparison, not recognising that straightening resolves the problem.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a curled piece of string and a straight one of the same length; stretch them both to show they are equal, then ask which looked longer before stretching; stretch: ask how they would compare two strings that cannot be removed from the wall.

exercise.description: Look at the string lights and help Adi choose the longest one; discuss how you found out.

items.section_title: Introducing the metre as a standard unit
items.prompt: Four children stand in a line. Rina is the tallest, Bharat is the shortest, and Gita and Mohan are in between. Only Rina and Gita are taller than one metre. Who is taller — Gita or Mohan? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Gita is taller than Mohan. Gita is taller than one metre and Mohan is not, so Gita's height is greater than one metre while Mohan's is less — Gita must be taller.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the one-metre mark as a common reference: Gita is above it and Mohan is below it, so Gita is taller.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a horizontal line for the one-metre mark and place the four children above or below it; stretch: ask whether you can tell how much taller Gita is than Mohan from this information, and why not.

exercise.description: Circle the tallest among the children shown and discuss how you decided.

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: Before cutting, each child in a group guesses how long one metre is and cuts a piece of thread. Then they check against the metre rope. Neel's thread is 10 cm shorter than a metre. Sita's thread is 5 cm shorter. Raj's thread is exactly one metre. Who made the best estimate?

options.label: A
options.text: All three estimated equally well.

options.label: B
options.text: Neel, because a shorter thread uses less wool.

options.label: C
options.text: Raj, because his thread matches the metre rope exactly.

options.label: D
options.text: Sita, because being a little short is always better.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Raj — option B. His thread matches the metre rope exactly, meaning zero difference between his estimate and the actual metre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The best estimate is the one with the smallest difference from the actual metre — zero difference is closest.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child introduced an irrelevant criterion (wool economy) rather than accuracy of estimation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child assumed a direction of error is preferable, not recognising that the goal is the smallest gap from the target.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child did not compare the size of the differences and concluded all were equal.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the three differences (10 cm, 5 cm, 0 cm) and ask which number is smallest; stretch: if Sita had been 2 cm short instead of 5 cm, would she have beaten Raj? Why or why not?

exercise.description: Estimate and cut a one-metre long wool or thread; verify with the metre rope whose estimate is closest.

items.prompt: A line is drawn below that is 6 cm long. Which of the following correctly describes a line that is longer than this line?

options.label: A
options.text: A line that is 2 cm long.

options.label: B
options.text: A line that is 4 cm long.

options.label: C
options.text: A line that is 6 cm long.

options.label: D
options.text: A line that is 9 cm long.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A line that is 9 cm long — option C. 9 is greater than 6, so a 9 cm line is longer than the given 6 cm line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the length values: a number greater than 6 means the line is longer.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child chose 4 cm, which is shorter than 6 cm — a reversal of the direction of comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child chose 6 cm — the same length, not longer.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child chose 2 cm, which is much shorter — likely a random choice or a misreading of 'longer' as 'shorter'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two lines of the stated lengths and ask the child to point to the longer one; stretch: ask the child to name the length of a line that would be longer than 9 cm and shorter than 12 cm.

exercise.description: Draw a string longer than the string given below.

items.prompt: Shelly and Adi are holding a decoration string that is 8 cm long. Which line below is shorter than their string?

options.label: A
options.text: A line that is 10 cm long.

options.label: B
options.text: A line that is 12 cm long.

options.label: C
options.text: A line that is 5 cm long.

options.label: D
options.text: A line that is 8 cm long.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A line that is 5 cm long — option C. 5 is less than 8, so a 5 cm line is shorter than the 8 cm decoration string.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare values: a number less than 8 gives a shorter line.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child chose 10 cm, which is longer than 8 cm — reversed the direction of comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child chose 12 cm, which is even longer — same reversal error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child chose 8 cm — the same length, not shorter.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: point to each value on the number line stimulus and ask 'is this smaller or bigger than 8?' before making a choice; stretch: ask the child to give two more lengths that would also be shorter than 8 cm.

exercise.description: Draw a string shorter than the decoration string Shelly and Adi are holding.

items.prompt: A rectangular board has a top edge of 5 unit-strings and a side edge of 2 unit-strings. How many unit-strings are needed to go all the way around the border of the board?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 14 unit-strings. The border has four sides: 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the four sides of the rectangle: top + right side + bottom + left side = 5 + 2 + 5 + 2.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the rectangle, label each side, and add one side at a time; stretch: ask how many unit-strings would be saved if only three sides of the board were decorated.

exercise.description: How many of the given unit-string are needed to decorate the entire border of the board?

items.section_title: Measuring with metre, half metre, and quarter metre
items.prompt: Tara has a rope that is one metre long. She wants to cut it into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts does she need to make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 cuts. The first cut produces 2 pieces, the second cut makes 3 pieces, and the third cut makes 4 pieces — three cuts in total.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each cut adds one new piece; starting with 1 piece, three cuts produce 1 + 3 = 4 pieces.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a straight line and ask the child to mark where the cuts go, then count the marks; stretch: ask how many cuts would be needed to make 6 equal pieces.

exercise.description: Cut a one-metre rope into 4 equal pieces. How many cuts did you make?
